CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Engage the diplomatic track decisively now that Trump and Xi have agreed to meet at the G20 in Buenos Aires, and come to that meeting with serious, concrete purchase and market-opening proposals in order to forestall the scheduled January 1 escalation of the $200B tariff list from 10% to 25% and to stop further expansion of Section 301 coverage. Avoid fresh retaliation that would hand Washington a pretext to proceed with the January hike, while preserving our own retaliatory capacity as leverage. This is the moment to negotiate, not to escalate or capitulate.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high: US Section 301 tariffs now cover roughly $250B of Chinese exports at 10%, with an automatic rise to 25% on January 1, 2019, and Trump has signaled willingness to extend coverage to essentially all Chinese shipments (event timeline: List 1-3 effective July/Aug/Sept; List 3 finalized Sept 18, effective Sept 24; earlier $50B at 25%). This directly hits major export sectors, and the ZTE denial order (April) shows firm-level/entity-list targeting that threatens our tech self-sufficiency ambitions. Macro evidence confirms the economy is already feeling the strain: the yuan has depreciated roughly 9% since April, the PBOC is injecting liquidity (RRR cut on Oct 8), and economists warn of capital-outflow and further-depreciation risk, with our own leadership publicly ruling out devaluation as a tool. That combination — export tariffs, FX pressure, and a cooling domestic economy — supports a threat score at the +0.5 'high' anchor rather than existential, because we retain large reserves, retaliation capacity, and a non-tariff response menu. The action stance is deliberately measured: with a Trump-Xi summit agreed for late November (web evidence, Oct 11), the highest-value move is to negotiate seriously and secure a delay/stay of the January escalation, which escalation would only accelerate. Fetching a deal at Buenos Aires is more protective of our export economy than mirror-escalation at this juncture, so we hold at negotiate with a mildly de-escalatory tilt rather than concede purchases prematurely — a full purchase commitment should await matching US concessions.
key_factors: Section 301 tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese exports; $200B list set to rise 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
Scheduled escalation and threat of full ~$505B coverage create material export-sector hit
Yuan down ~9% since April; PBOC RRR cut (Oct 8); capital-outflow and depreciation concerns
ZTE denial order sets entity-list precedent threatening tech self-sufficiency
Trump-Xi G20 Buenos Aires meeting agreed (Oct 11) — a concrete off-ramp
China retains FX reserves, non-tariff retaliation options, and domestic market as buffers

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs on ~$60B. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B.
USTR publishes finalized List 3... scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order).
China is pouring more cash into its flagging economy... under pressure from US tariffs on more than $250 billion of Chinese exports... yuan is down almost 6% against the dollar this year.
The yuan has dropped sharply... losing about 9% of its value since April... 'China will never go down the path of stimulating exports by devaluing its currency.'
President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping have agreed to meet next month at the G-20 summit in Buenos Aires.
